title: EXISTS and NOT EXISTS
objective: Test whether related rows exist (or don't) with EXISTS / NOT EXISTS. They are NULL-safe, duplicate-free and the standard tool for anti-joins and data-quality checks.
context: Data quality and lifecycle questions are existence questions: customers who never ordered, orders without items, orders pointing to missing customers, suppliers with no products. EXISTS answers them cleanly, without NOT IN's NULL trap or a LEFT JOIN's duplicates.

exercises.title: Customers who have ordered
exercises.question: How many of our customers have placed any order at all, and who are they?
exercises.prompt: Return customer_id, name for customers with at least one order of any status, using EXISTS.
hints: The outer table is customers; the inner one is orders.
Correlate inside: WHERE o.customer_id = c.customer_id.
WHERE EXISTS (SELECT 1 FROM orders o WHERE o.customer_id = c.customer_id)
exercises.why: A semi-join keeps each customer once. A plain JOIN would return customer 1 nine times.

recall.q: Does the SELECT list inside EXISTS matter?
recall.a: No. Only whether at least one row exists. SELECT 1 is convention.

exercises.title: Customers who never ordered
exercises.question: Marketing wants a welcome-offer list of signed-up customers who have never ordered.
exercises.prompt: Return customer_id, name, signup_date for customers with no orders of any status, using NOT EXISTS.
hints: Same as the previous exercise, with NOT.
WHERE NOT EXISTS (SELECT 1 FROM orders o WHERE ...)
SELECT c.customer_id, c.name, c.signup_date FROM customers c WHERE NOT EXISTS (SELECT 1 FROM orders o WHERE o.customer_id = c.customer_id);
exercises.why: Customers 18, 19 and 20 are the activation audience. Note that 19 ('alice johnson') may be a duplicate of customer 1, which is worth flagging before you email them.

recall.q: Name three ways to find customers with no orders.
recall.a: NOT EXISTS, LEFT JOIN ... WHERE o.order_id IS NULL, and NOT IN (with a NULL-free subquery).

exercises.title: Orders with no line items
exercises.question: Data engineering wants to catch order headers that have no lines.
exercises.prompt: Return order_id, order_date, order_status for orders that have no rows in order_items.
hints: Outer: orders. Inner: order_items.
Correlate on order_id.
WHERE NOT EXISTS (SELECT 1 FROM order_items i WHERE i.order_id = o.order_id)
exercises.why: Header-without-lines rows inflate order counts while adding no revenue, which drags AOV down. Order 60 is pending, so it may simply be mid-checkout, but it should be monitored.

recall.q: Is an order with no items counted by COUNT(*) FROM orders?
recall.a: Yes, which is why such orphans distort per-order metrics.

exercises.title: Orphan orders (customer missing)
exercises.question: Finance found revenue that doesn't tie to any customer. Which orders point to a non-existent customer?
exercises.prompt: Return order_id, customer_id, order_date, order_status for orders whose customer_id has no matching row in customers.
hints: This time the outer table is orders and the inner one is customers.
Referential-integrity check: does a parent row exist for this child?
WHERE NOT EXISTS (SELECT 1 FROM customers c WHERE c.customer_id = o.customer_id)
exercises.why: Order 31 (customer 99) is a completed order worth $363.30 that disappears from any report that inner-joins orders to customers. Orphan checks belong in every data-quality suite.

recall.q: Which report numbers change when orphan orders exist?
recall.a: Any revenue joined through customers (by region, by segment) is lower than the total from orders alone.

exercises.title: Suppliers with no products (NULL-safe)
exercises.question: Procurement asks again: which suppliers supply none of our products? This time, no traps.
exercises.prompt: Return supplier_id, supplier_name for suppliers with no product in products, using NOT EXISTS (products.supplier_id contains a NULL; NOT EXISTS is unaffected).
hints: Compare with exercise 21.4, where NOT IN returned nothing.
The NULL supplier_id row simply never matches p.supplier_id = s.supplier_id, so no harm done.
WHERE NOT EXISTS (SELECT 1 FROM products p WHERE p.supplier_id = s.supplier_id)
exercises.why: This is the habit to keep: reach for NOT EXISTS for anti-joins and you never hit the NOT IN NULL bug.

recall.q: Why is NOT EXISTS NULL-safe while NOT IN is not?
recall.a: NOT EXISTS only asks whether a matching row exists; a NULL just fails to match. NOT IN compares against every value, and a comparison with NULL makes the whole test unknown.

exercises.title: First-time buyers in 2025
exercises.question: Growth wants customers whose first valid purchase happened in 2025, i.e. they bought in 2025 but never in 2024.
exercises.prompt: Return customer_id, name for customers who have at least one valid order (valid orders = order_status IN ('completed','shipped','returned'); cancelled and pending are excluded) dated in 2025 and no valid order dated in 2024. Customer 16, whose only order was cancelled, must not appear.
hints: Two existence tests on the same customer: EXISTS for 2025, NOT EXISTS for 2024.
Put the status and date filters inside each subquery.
WHERE EXISTS (... <valid> AND order_date in 2025) AND NOT EXISTS (... <valid> AND order_date in 2024)
exercises.why: 'Did X but never Y' is the shape of acquisition, churn and cross-sell lists. Customer 13 signed up in 2024 but first bought in 2025, so signup date is not first purchase.

recall.q: How do you express 'did A but never did B' in SQL?

exercises.title: Buyers who never needed a refund
exercises.question: The reviews team wants to invite happy customers: those with valid orders and no refunded items, ever.
exercises.prompt: Return customer_id, name for customers who have at least one valid order (valid orders = order_status IN ('completed','shipped','returned'); cancelled and pending are excluded) and for whom no order (any status) contains an order_item that appears in returns.
hints: The NOT EXISTS subquery has to walk orders → order_items → returns.
Correlate only on the customer: WHERE o.customer_id = c.customer_id.
... AND NOT EXISTS (SELECT 1 FROM orders o JOIN order_items i ON ... JOIN returns r ON r.order_item_id = i.order_item_id WHERE o.customer_id = c.customer_id)
exercises.why: The inner query of EXISTS can be as complex as you need, with joins included. The outer result still never duplicates customers.

recall.q: Can the subquery inside EXISTS contain joins?
recall.a: Yes. Any query works; only 'at least one row?' is evaluated.

worked_example.question: Which products have been sold in a cancelled order?
worked_example.sql:
SELECT p.product_id, p.product_name
FROM products AS p
WHERE EXISTS (SELECT 1
              FROM order_items AS i
              JOIN orders AS o ON o.order_id = i.order_id
              WHERE i.product_id = p.product_id
                AND o.order_status = 'cancelled')
LIMIT 5;
worked_example.explanation: The inner query can join and filter like any query. It is correlated on product_id. Each product appears once even if it was in several cancelled orders.

recipe:
**Recipe: 'is there at least one matching row?'**

1. Start from the entity you want to return: `SELECT c.customer_id FROM customers AS c`.
2. Add `WHERE [NOT] EXISTS (SELECT 1 FROM orders AS o WHERE o.customer_id = c.customer_id [AND ...extra conditions])`.
3. The SELECT list inside doesn't matter (`SELECT 1` is the convention). Only whether a row exists matters.
   ```sql
   SELECT c.customer_id, c.name
   FROM customers AS c
   WHERE NOT EXISTS (SELECT 1 FROM orders AS o WHERE o.customer_id = c.customer_id);
   ```
4. **NULL-safe:** a NULL in the inner table just doesn't match, so NOT EXISTS never collapses to "no rows"
   the way NOT IN does.
5. **No duplicates:** each outer row is kept at most once, however many matches exist (unlike a JOIN).
6. Combine freely: `EXISTS (...) AND NOT EXISTS (...)` = "did X but never did Y".
snowflake_notes:
- EXISTS / NOT EXISTS are identical in Snowflake and are usually optimised into semi-joins / anti-joins.
- Snowflake has no `LEFT ANTI JOIN` keyword (Spark does). Write NOT EXISTS, or LEFT JOIN ... WHERE right.key IS NULL.
common_mistakes: Forgetting the correlation (`WHERE o.customer_id = c.customer_id`): EXISTS becomes true for every row (or false for all).
Using NOT IN when the inner column can be NULL. Prefer NOT EXISTS.
Replacing EXISTS with a JOIN and getting duplicates of the outer rows.
Putting conditions (status, date) outside the subquery when they describe the inner rows.
Inner-joining orders to customers in a revenue report and silently losing orphan order 31.
recall: What's the difference between a semi-join and an anti-join?
Semi-join keeps outer rows WITH a match (EXISTS); anti-join keeps those WITHOUT (NOT EXISTS).
Why is EXISTS often preferred to IN for big tables?
It can stop at the first match, and NOT EXISTS is NULL-safe; optimizers handle both well.
Give two data-quality checks you can write with NOT EXISTS.
Orders without items; orders whose customer doesn't exist (orphans).
